papers.title: High fidelity control of superconducting qubits with optical transmitted signal
papers.abstract: Superconducting circuits exhibit remarkable potential for constructing large-scale quantum simulation and computation systems, featuring numerous qubits, extended coherence time, and precise control. Nevertheless, the growing number of signal cables poses a challenge in dilution refrigerators due to space and heat load constraints. To overcome this issue, we experimentally implemented an optically-assisted transmission line as an alternative to coaxial cables. By modulating microwave signals on laser intensities at room temperature and regenerating the signals at a cryogenic plate within the dilution refrigerator, we demonstrated full control of superconducting qubits using photocurrent. We demonstrate and benchmark both single-qubit and two-qubit gates on frequency tunable transmon qubits, achieving fidelities of 99.915% $\pm$ 0.005% and 99.676% $\pm$ 0.041%, respectively, which have reached the requirement of the surface code.

Quantum Computer Controlled by Superconducting Digital Electronics at Millikelvin Temperature

summary.summary: This work demonstrates optical-assisted transmission of microwave control signals for superconducting qubits, modulating XY and Z control signals on a 1490 nm directly modulated laser at room temperature and regenerating them with InGaAs photodiodes at the 4 K stage of a dilution refrigerator. Single-qubit and two-qubit CZ gates achieve fidelities of 99.915% ± 0.005% and 99.676% ± 0.041%, respectively, meeting surface-code error-correction thresholds while reducing heat load and enabling thousand-channel scalability.
summary.motivation: Scaling superconducting quantum processors to thousands of qubits faces a critical bottleneck: the growing number of microwave control cables creates excessive heat load and spatial constraints in dilution refrigerators. Optical transmission offers dramatically reduced passive heat load compared to coaxial cables (5.6 μW versus ~1 mW at 4 K per line), enabling orders-of-magnitude improvement in channel density.
summary.method: A directly modulated distributed feedback laser at 1490 nm carries IQ-mixed XY signals and Z square-wave pulses from room temperature through optical fiber to InGaAs PIN photodiodes (reverse-biased at 1 V) mounted at the 4 K stage, which regenerate microwave control signals. Gate optimization uses standard Ramsey and cross-entropy benchmarking techniques; noise is characterized via RTO and CPMG sequences on the qubit and room-temperature instrumentation spanning 10$^{-3}$ to 10$^7$ Hz.
summary.result: Measured $T_1 = 58.58 ± 3.39$ μs and $T_2^* = 2.40 ± 0.23$ μs; single-qubit 50 ns X/2 gates with control error 0.004%–0.023%; two-qubit 38 ns CZ gate with control error 0.053%; Z-line noise floor ~0.04% idle-gate error at 10$^{-3}$ Hz; thermal analysis shows 4 K stage can support ~2000 channels for XY+Z control, matching the $P_C/P_L$ ratio of 1996 for the Bluefors XLD400 refrigerator.

papers.title: Provably Efficient Self-Calibrating Quantum Fault Tolerance
papers.abstract: Quantum error correction protects logical information only when every physical operation remains below the fault-tolerance threshold, a condition that must be maintained continuously rather than only at the initial calibration. In practice, however, analog control parameters inevitably drift because of environmental fluctuations. As future fault-tolerant quantum computations are expected to run for days or even months, interrupting computation for repeated recalibration becomes fundamentally impractical. A promising alternative is to integrate calibration directly into computation by repurposing syndrome measurements as a calibration signal (Sivak et al, Nature 2026), but whether such self-calibration can be achieved with provable efficiency remains an open question. Here we establish a theoretical framework for such self-calibrating quantum fault tolerance. We prove that, for a broad class of control-induced errors, the detection rate defines a locally strongly convex surrogate objective for analog calibration with high probability. This geometric property enables a simple and efficient online optimization algorithm using only syndrome measurements collected during normal error correction. We prove convergence to an $\varepsilon$ detection rate within $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ epochs for time-independent drifts and also establish guarantees for time-dependent drifts. We further show that the convergence rate is independent of the code distance for quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. Pulse-level simulations of neutral-atom arrays and large-scale circuit-level Clifford simulations confirm these theoretical predictions. Our results establish self-calibrating fault tolerance as a provably efficient paradigm in which the same syndrome measurements simultaneously protect logical information and stabilize the underlying hardware.

summary.summary: This paper establishes a theoretical framework for self-calibrating quantum fault tolerance, proving that syndrome measurements collected during quantum error correction can simultaneously protect logical information and stabilize hardware control parameters. The framework proves convergence to $\varepsilon$ detection rate within $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ epochs for time-independent drifts and demonstrates code-distance-independent scalability for quantum LDPC codes.
summary.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires continuous maintenance of control parameters below error thresholds, yet environmental drift is unavoidable over computation timescales of days to months. Interrupting computation for recalibration is impractical, motivating integration of calibration into the QEC cycle itself using syndrome measurements as calibration signals.
summary.method: The authors prove that the detector-event rate defines a locally strongly convex surrogate objective for analog calibration after randomized compiling, enabling zeroth-order online optimization. They implement projected SPSA for time-independent drifts and online projected SPSA for time-dependent drifts, with locality-aware variants for surface codes and quantum LDPC codes that achieve convergence independent of code distance.
summary.result: Pulse-level simulations of neutral-atom Rydberg gates on the $[[4,1,2]]$ code confirm $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ convergence. Circuit-level Clifford simulations on rotated surface codes (distance $d=3$–$13$) and bivariate-bicycle codes show calibrated detection rates dropping from $\sim 0.09$–$0.10$ to $\sim 0.014$–$0.021$ within 2000 iterations, with locality-aware SPSA matching or outperforming reinforcement-learning baselines while maintaining performance independent of $d$.

papers.title: Coherence protection of a silicon hole spin qubit with phase-modulated microwave driving
papers.abstract: Hole spins in silicon quantum dots are a promising platform for quantum computing due to their strong intrinsic spin-orbit coupling (SOC), which enables fast, all-electrical control. However, this coupling also increases their susceptibility to charge noise, thereby limiting coherence times. Moreover, holes in silicon are also affected by hyperfine interactions with residual nuclear spins in the silicon substrate, introducing a non-negligible source of low-frequency noise. Here, we implement a phase-modulated concatenated continuous driving (CCD) technique for hole spin qubits to suppress low-frequency noise through microwave phase modulation. This approach stabilizes Rabi oscillations and extends the oscillation decay time compared to the conventional method. Furthermore, by defining a qubit in the CCD frame, we achieve coherent control while simultaneously protecting the qubit from noise, confirming coherence protection during gate operations. These results demonstrate a viable route toward noise-robust hole spin qubits.

summary.summary: A phase-modulated concatenated continuous driving (CCD) technique suppresses low-frequency charge and hyperfine noise in hole spin qubits in silicon quantum dots. The method stabilizes Rabi oscillations, extends decay times, and maintains coherence protection during gate operations.
summary.motivation: Hole spins in silicon benefit from strong spin-orbit coupling for fast electrical control, but this same coupling makes them susceptible to charge noise and hyperfine interactions with residual nuclear spins, limiting coherence times.
summary.method: Phase modulation of microwave driving was applied using a concatenated continuous driving protocol to suppress low-frequency noise while maintaining qubit control in the CCD frame.
summary.result: The phase-modulated CCD technique extended Rabi oscillation decay times compared to conventional driving and demonstrated coherence protection during gate operations.
